summary: Three small corrections. The quoted translation of Castiglione didn't match any published wording, so it now uses George Bull's; the Oxford English Dictionary's definition is longer than two words; and the recall question had Clever Hans's figures muddled (98 and 8 per cent, as No. 2 now says, not 89 and 6). Everything else checked out.

changes.before: 'a certain nonchalance, so as to conceal all art'
changes.after: 'a certain nonchalance which conceals all artistry'
changes.why: No published translation has the words as quoted. Singleton's reads 'a certain sprezzatura, so as to conceal all art'; George Bull's modern Penguin translation (1967) reads 'a certain nonchalance which conceals all artistry'.

changes.before: The Oxford English Dictionary now defines sprezzatura in two words: 'studied carelessness'.
changes.after: The Oxford English Dictionary's definition of sprezzatura includes the phrase 'studied carelessness'.
changes.why: The OED definition is longer than two words: 'ease of manner, studied carelessness; the appearance of acting or being done without effort'.

changes.before: Clever Hans the horse answered correctly 89 per cent of the time when his questioner knew the answer.
changes.after: Clever Hans the horse answered correctly 98 per cent of the time when his questioner knew the answer.
changes.why: Pfungst reports 98% correct when the questioner knew the answer and 8% when they didn't; 89% and 6% are from the blinker test. No. 2 was corrected to these figures on its re-check.

changes.before: Only 6 per cent of the time.
changes.after: Only 8 per cent of the time.
changes.why: Same correction, so the recall matches Pfungst and No. 2.

notes: The Opdycke translation in further reading is dated 1902 on its title page (London: Duckworth; New York: Scribner), though it was copyrighted in 1901 and some catalogues list it as 1901. I left 1902.
Ovid's words 'ars adeo latet arte sua' are genuine, but classicists debate whether the text is sound (Korenjak 2020, Panegyres 2022 in The Classical Quarterly). The story's gloss is a fair reading.
The Looking-Glass is right that replications of Kruger's poem and painting studies were mixed (Ziano and colleagues, 2023): the painting result replicated once, the poem result didn't.

Two links opened at a different address showing the same page: the Wikipedia article (via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Courtier) and The Classical Quarterly note (via Cambridge's core-cms address; the cambridge.org address itself was refused to my tools).
